Shopping at Aldi saves me about 40 percent over what it would cost to shop at a major grocery store chain.

The reason Aldi has such low prices is because they have gotten rid of a lot of the frills that cost consumers money at many other grocery stores. 

You have to insert a quarter into the chain-locked shopping cart to release it, and if you don't return the cart, you can't get your quarter back.  So there are no employees whose job is to chase shopping carts around parking lots.

You bag your own groceries and bring your own bags. Otherwise, you buy the bags from Aldi or dump all the food in the trunk of your car loose. So there are no employees who are "baggers." You are the bagger.

There are few name brand items at Aldi. Nearly all the items are Aldi house brands. Most taste the same as the name brands.

There is no music playing. Music costs money.

There are no loyalty cards, and Aldi does not accept coupons. 

The range of items available is smaller than in larger grocery stores, and not all items are available all the time. On the other hand, sometimes there are gourmet items at a deep discount.

I get the vast majority of my grocery shopping done at Aldi, and when they don't have what I need, I go elsewhere. That is fine by me. I guess you could just call it buying the steak, not the sizzle.

The debate must not only take into account the environmental hazards and competition for scare resources caused by A.I. data centers, but the dangers posed by A.I. itself.

Especially on foreign trips, Air Force One is not a lone aircraft. It is the visible center of a larger airborne and logistical machine: backup aircraft, cargo planes, communications platforms, refueling support and, when needed, the E-4B “Doomsday” plane, a flying command post built for the worst imaginable scenarios. The system is designed around redundancy, continuity and survival.
So perhaps the pearl-clutching can be retired. If Democrats want to criticize the President, they should do it honestly and directly. But pretending that his travel arrangements are some reckless gamble only exposes how little they understand about the machinery that protects the office, no matter who occupies it.

One Hundred Years - 1921-2021

You entered New York Harbor—all alone 

The New Colossus summoned you ashore, 

A Lady, versus brazen Greek Sun God   

Her beacon flame, a mighty light— a chance, 

Her Tabula Ansata and Torch—fixed

And carried high— an immortal Bonjour

Her steadfast gaze, you said, emitted strength,  

Despite a bitter January wind

That slapped your cheeks as if to say, “Go Home!”   

The evening stars above said— Home, at Last.           

From Village Einsiedel to Port of Trieste,   

Then New York Harbor— a girl, just turned

Fourteen— a Birthday without Cake or Song,

But breathed by the Mother of Exiles.

  

You carried five languages on your tongue.

None of them English, but knew you could learn

What it meant to be an American.

A Century later, and you’re still gone,

But my words here serve to prove you are not,  

You mothered and grandmothered all your life,

For us, you scrubbed, and soothed, made Plum Dumplings,

My Lady of the Harbor, you were and are 

So much more— so, “I lift my lamp” to thee” and    

Imagine where you began, and begin,

A winged Colossus, singing Emma’s song.

Thank you for this opinion piece.

“Gun violence” as a phrase, is sloppy because it obscures and misleads. It removes context. A substantial number of informed people are instinctively repulsed by the use of the term.

Kill someone with a gun? – Gun violence.  Legitimately kill someone in self-defense using a gun? – Gun violence. Commit suicide with a gun? – Gun violence. Accidentally shoot someone with a gun? – Gun violence.  Wound someone with a gun? – Gun violence. Shoot a gun, even if you miss, to stop someone from attacking you? – Gun violence. Threaten someone with a gun? – Gun violence.  Yet, as we all know, circumstances can vary, and not all uses of a gun constitute a crime.

Depending on the definition, the term “gun violence” can allow one to exaggerate the truth, and thus scare the ignorant into supporting restrictions on the right of self-defense, because, after all, who, in their right mind, could possibly be against gun violence?

comments.name: Andrew Szakmary
comments.body: Of course, renewables like solar and wind will replace fossil fuels if they are cheaper. However, I am not quite convinced that this is the case in the U.S. now or in the near future. Firstly, we have abundant natural gas, and the cost of gas here is significantly less than in Europe or Asia where it must be imported as LNG. Moreover, gas power plants are very flexible, making it easy to scale up and scale down production as needed to meet demand, in contrast to solar and wind, where production is intermittent and  generally uncorrelated with electricity demand, requiring huge battery storage capacity to make it work. Yes, battery prices are falling, but they are still high. If someone can produce detailed financial analysis, using reasonable assumptions for the cost of capital, showing that the equivalent annual cost (which takes into account the much larger up-front capital investment) of generating electricity from solar or wind is lower than that from using gas, I’m all in. However, this article does not do that.

Moreover, Ezra was right to note that Stanford's Mark Jacobson is the "most optimistic" of the renewable energy modelers -- so optimistic, in fact, that he sued a number of other academics in 2017 who found major flaws in one of his major "optimistic" studies -- and he rightly lost. comments.body: As someone who has been engaged with environmental, climate, and clean energy efforts for a while, I absolutely love the good news that is emerging.  We have solar panels on our roof that cover 100% of our electric needs some months, including charging a car, so I am also living evidence of that story!  I have generally been engaged with left-leaning environmental organizations, but with all the economic evidence and arguments for energy independence, this seems like a really good time to cast a wider net and work with individuals and organizations on the other side of the political spectrum to share this good news.  I believe that by identifying common goals - and I do believe those exist - and working together we can make more permanent change rather than enacting partisan policy that is reversed as soon as political control switches hands.  As well as continuing to work in the environmental world, I have become involved with Braver Angels, a national organization dedicated to building bridges across the aisle through respectful dialogue.  I truly believe that healing the divides in our country is the way forward and would love to see Ezra in conversation with Maury Giles from Braver Angels.  I would also love to know what others, especially in the environmental world, think about the possibility of collaborations between liberal, conservative, and neutral organizations.

It is fair and reasonable to attribute a lack of coherence to much of what we are seeing from this Administration, as regards to the lurching instability that, daily, appears on display. 

However, I think a Plan C has been in operation all along, since the first cessation of widespread hostilities. 

Regardless of what President Trump has said about the conflict, the U.S. military has always been fully aware of the danger and capacity of Iran to inflict damage on vessels traversing the Strait. 

There may be a number of approaches one could take to reduce Iran’s capacity along these lines, but something most of these scenarios will have in common is reducing and consistently pushing back Iran’s physical access to the Strait, surrounding areas north and south, as far as possible from the coast. 

The initial strikes, numerous as they were, did not heavily concentrate disproportionately on the Strait and adjacent coastal areas. 

The impact of this strategy became immediately apparent as the initial cease fire(s) took hold — Iran still had more than sufficient capability in the area to halt traffic on the Strait. 

What to do?

comments.body:
We should all be concerned about water use, but large data centers do not inherently require enormous quantities of fresh water. A facility near Oklahoma City could economically use sealed direct-to-chip cooling loops, dry coolers that reject heat to the air, and treated wastewater only as optional backup during extreme heat. Properly designed, such a facility could reduce potable-water consumption by more than 90% compared with conventional evaporative cooling, potentially using almost no drinking water for routine cooling.

Unfortunately, much of the public commentary treats every water-cooled system as though it continuously consumes the water circulating inside it. That reflects either a misunderstanding of closed-loop cooling or an ulterior motive to oppose the project regardless of its design. The responsible position is not to dismiss water concerns, but to require enforceable water-use limits, prohibit routine potable-water cooling, and judge the proposed facility by its actual engineering rather than alarming assumptions.

The old production ( so idolized by right wing "Christians" as a model for living) was so sickeningly sweet, and so far from the books, that I couldn't bear watching it for more than the first 5 minutes.  I didn't think there could possibly be worse... but while a visually pleasing production, this one is far, far worse.  Laura Ingalls' account of her pioneer childhood (leaving out some of the most painful, least flattering parts, such as her family's having fled debt in the middle of the night, their acceptance of government relief when their crops failed, and the death of her baby brother) stands on its own as a valuable and true accounting of pioneer life in the 1870s and 80s, after the Civil War.  Her description of settlers' mixed feelings towards the Indians that they were replacing (most greatly fearing attack and death, her father expressing respect for some of them) was true to the reality of that time.  Her description of the African American doctor who saved them from dying of malaria was true to the time.  Her description of a blackface minstrel show was true to the time.

To now change the story to make it politically correct for the 21st century, with Native American and African American friends, neighbors, and business associates integrated into the wholly invented plot, is so untrue to the original books that it really shouldn't bear the "Little House" name.  And is it really necessary for Ma to mouth the theme, "We'll always be together" so many times?

We have entered a time here in the great, ol' U-S-A where if you are not rich, you are dog meat. Really. Everything at every corner is being slanted to the wealthy and cutting off some "perks" to save a couple a hundred on an international flight brings no thrills.

All of this adds up to my flight to my vacation being something that I can enjoy rather than something that I have to endure until my vacation actually starts. Absolutely terrifying. This scenario is my worst nightmare. 

The terrain and weather in San Diego are similar--and we're at risk of the same wind-driven blazes.

I wish more people had my life experience of watching a rapid change in seasonal weather patterns.

I grew up in Flagstaff, Arizona--a mountain town in a pine forest at 7000-foot elevation.

Today, winters are much milder and warmer. The pine trees are dying in droves. Animals, plants, and insects seen at lower altitudes are now common. 

Remember the Road Runner (Beep Beep!) getting chased past desert cactus by Wile E. Coyote? Well, the Road Runner is now in the forest! 

It feels as if Flagstaff slid down a hill by about 1000 feet--and fell into a different life zone. 

Every community is built around its regular climate. When the climate changes within 50 years--from low alpine to high desert--there is a cascade of problems.

No one needed AC in the summer when I was growing up as the nighttime lows were often in the 40’s to low 50’s--and high temperatures were less frequent. But now, the lows are almost 60 degrees, the monsoon rains are scarce, and daytime temps often reach over 85 F.

If there is this much change in the next 50 years, all the pine forest will die—and that will mean massive fires in Northern Arizona towns as this transition from forest to desert happens.

At this rate, we won’t need to travel to Mars to find a desiccated desert world. We are building it here with our own CO2 pollution…

They have a website where you can see hours of videos from areas where no human is likely to ever be able to explore in person, due to the extremes of pressure. When they are operating an ROV mission, you can watch in real time and hear the discussions from the onboard teams, world class oceanographers and marine biologists. You can also find the videos and the live feeds on YouTube - look for "Okeanos Redux" channel. Science fiction: "We have bizarre life forms that thrive in conditions that would instantly destroy humans." Deep ocean: "Hold my beer."
The Trump regime has already slashed the budget and staffing of NOAA. It's partly because NOAA routinely records hard evidence of climate change and makes the data public, but it's also because NOAA keeps finding reasons to be very cautious about commercializing and industrializing the deep ocean.
Write (or call or text or email) your Congressional Representatives and Senators and tell them that you want them to support continuing funding and staffing of NOAA. If they don't hear from voters, they will figure that their constituents don't care.

comments.name: smartguitar
comments.body: There's another wrinkle to Foucault's essay on "The Death of the Author" that this article doesn't fully address:  the birth of the author.  Foucault was particularly interested in the 17th and 18th centuries, a period when anonymity gave way to individuality--to the bourgeois subject, a socially constructed figure.  While we can obviously find an AI dimension to Foucault's much discussed essay, the birth of the author--a seemingly unique, autonomous individual who was, in fact, a social construction--was his primary point.   With the rise of AI, as much as we might mourn the death of this individual, we must also realize that it was always something of a fiction.  Before AI, we thought we were more unique than we were.

comments.name: Rick Wells
comments.body: Foucault molded my spatial view of history, allowing me to escape the minutiae of the narrative view. Forget Descartes, philosophical thought was modernized by the German idealists (Kant, Hegel, et al) and post-modern French thinkers such as Foucault, Deleuze, Derrida, et al. The British historian, Collingwood, wrote that history, in reduction, is "the history of thought". Like Einstein, Foucault transformed modern thought. This is "progress", and this article is merely a representation of Foucault's insightful view of Power and Control.

"The A.I. revolution was still more than 50 years off when Michel Foucault published his lecture “What Is an Author?” in 1969."

comments.name: Whatup Neighbor
comments.body:
There's a kind of cynical hopelessness in Foucault's perspective that reminds me of Southpark... a suspicious approach to every aspect of human life, with the assumption that even things that may appear objectively good on the surface (having children, pursuing an education) are merely channels through which power flow and which will only lead to something worse.

Confronting societal myths and ideologies, exploring their contradictions and failings, can be useful. But as I found out as a humanities grad student, tearing down, poking holes and critiquing ideas and institutions is the easy part--what's difficult is maintaining some sort of core beliefs that allow for the possibility of actual positive change in humanity. 

I never found that in Foucault, who, like the many grad students who came after him, seems more concerned with cleverly demonstrating how "everything sucks" than in looking at ways that things could be better.

comments.name: April Durham
comments.body: I would like to add that all this unpacking and reflective turning of Foucault and his contemporaries is ALSO pointing us to the possibility of asking different questions that perhaps allow subjects to lessen the hold of power that turns us into objects.  In his early book The Order of Things, Foucault considers Borges’ fantastical classification of animals as one model for escaping modes of thought that have captured us as we assume they are logical and “right.” Foucault’s friend and (also maligned) French philosopher Gilles Deleuze suggests we might escape similar thought patterns by entertaining the notion that 2+3 might NOT equal 5. While mathematically perhaps impossible, the mere act of consideration of the impossible allows for thought patterns and ensuing beliefs to be startled out of or dislodged from assumptions that they are “natural” and therefore correct.  While the chaos of today’s political and social landscape in the US and parts of Europe is terrifying, i do feel the challenge to power in these philosophers’ work is not a free fall into nihilistic soullessness, but to allow the disruptive perspective to give rise to difference in a way that foils these opposing discourses and that may allow a turn toward what could be life giving (or not, no guarantees) in the face of overwhelming odds.

Right to repair is one of the most powerful and effective ways consumers have to fight back against monopolistic corporations. If we lose the right to fix our own things, not only do they no longer belong to us, but we also submit ourselves to an inescapable cycle of purchasing devices designed to fail. It's no surprise that companies push so hard against this. I have an immense amount of respect for the EU's work on Right to Repair, especially mandating user-replacable parts and repair scores on products.

But let's not forget, the ultimate goal isn't that fixing things becomes cheap and easy. The ultimate goal is that fixing this isn't necessary in the first place! Companies absolutely could make their products last decades if they wanted. The washing machine my grandparents bought in the 80s has outlived the half dozen and counting in my childhood home. Our first fridge is working smoothly in the basement while the much newer one upstairs develops a series of strange issues.

We need to stop being so motivated by consumerism, appreciate what we have, and not be so tempted to buy shiny new things. Reward the companies who make things built to last.

The easiest way to break this cycle and bring about reliability again is powerful, enforced long-term minimum warranties. In the EU, most appliances now have a 10 year warranty by law. That's a much more important step in the right direction than any law allowing us to buy parts when these things break.

comments.body: Wow, can't recommend "All Night Long" enough for noir fans. A retelling of Othello set in swinging 60s London with Patrick McGoohan as the scheming Iago /jazz drummer working to break up Othello's band so singer Desdemona will join Iago's band. Cameos by Charles Mingus and Dave Brubeck as themselves at Richard Attenborough's after-hours party (they even play a too-brief duet), casual pot-smoking and two interracial relationships treated as no big deal--in 1962. Directed by the brilliant, daring British director Basil Dearden, this was his follow-up to the outstanding 1961 gay blackmail thriller Victim. It's a must-see, especially for noir fans who are also jazz fans. Thanks so much for this article, my watch list just grew by half a dozen films.

When I think of some of the ugly looks, done in name of art, that comes from high fashion, I want to shudder, not swoon. I wish myself back in a time when beauty, and also being able to live and breathe, in the clothes, mattered. 

Maybe the era of Jackie Kennedy. 

I am a person who loves beauty. Too many times, "edgy" means aggressive, to wit: the disturbing green ruffles under the emerald sequined gown. 

They look like ferns, but not nice ones, not pretty ones. I keep seeing death and decay in so much fashion.

Of course, nature can be lovely, but it can also be aggressive, dangerous and deeply off putting.

When fashion is inspired by nature, my preference is for beautiful, soothing and ethereal.

The flower gown is nice but it looks like a shower curtain in how it is designed, but I think many designers get this kind of look wrong. 

The top needs some kind of shape to it, maybe only a gentle suggestion of a shape, but to just let it hang down like that is not particularly elegant, even on a model. 

I wish edgy didn't always seem to mean absurd and aggressive, and off putting and dopey. 

As for our times not needing beauty and comfort, I do, very much, beg to disagree.

I think our current terms are covid - on steroids.

Ady Fidelin's story is an epic one: Man Ray had an editorial contract with Harper's Bazaar in the 1930s and sent in some photographs for a millinery feature in 1937; Fidelin was the model and it makes her the first Black woman to appear in an editorial feature in a fashion magazine. (September 1937 I think).

Fidelin was also the one who preserved Ray's archives after May 1940. A catalogue essay from a Centre Pompidou career retrospective on him in the 1980s mentioned her role but said she'd died. She hadn't. She was living quietly in Lyon.

There's also a link between a famed Picasso painting that I think is still held by his heirs and rarely lent out for exhibition that is strikingly similar to a lighthearted photo of Fidelin with a washboard-cum-skirt.

Finally, she is believed to have left Guadeloupe after losing her mother in the same hurricane Zora Neale Hurston describes. There's still a ton of birth/death records with her family name on the island. 

She was brilliant, beautiful, hyperorganized, adventurous, and nearly forgotten forever.

comments.name: Marie Bardos
comments.body: I don’t remember what year it was, but a friend and her daughter took a tour that included Tehran.  Not too long after the expulsion of the Shah.  My friend, a mystery addict like me, took a lot of books from my hoard of mysteries, so she could read them on the tour.  She was also a smoker and would leave guided tours in Tehran to sit outside so she could smoke.  She wasn't too careful about wearing a head scarf as required. People on the street would engage her in conversation and many asked if they could have some of her mysteries (from my hoard) when she finished them. The books were all in English, from England and the U.S. They ended up taking almost all of the hoard. Didn’t return any because they passed them on to other Iranians, who in turn passed them on so they were read by a great number of locals and who knows who else.
